{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Traumatic brain injury (moderate-to-severe, with altered mental status and drowsiness)", "confidence": 0.95}, {"diagnosis": "Tension pneumothorax", "confidence": 0.92}, {"diagnosis": "Acute traumatic aortic rupture", "confidence": 0.88}, {"diagnosis": "Flail chest with pulmonary contusion", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Hypovolemic shock secondary to intra-abdominal hemorrhage", "confidence": 0.78}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 0.134, "reasoning": "The patient presents <20 minutes post-high-speed MVC with classic red-flag symptoms: rapidly progressive drowsiness/confusion (suggesting cerebral hypoperfusion or direct intracranial injury), acute respiratory distress (indicating thoracic or upper airway compromise), and facial lacerations (marker of significant impact force). Tension pneumothorax is highly likely given acute dyspnea and altered mentation—causing hypoxia, hypercarbia, and reduced venous return leading to cerebral hypoperfusion. Traumatic brain injury is nearly certain given the mechanism and neurologic deterioration without obvious external head trauma (e.g., diffuse axonal injury or evolving epidural/subdural hematoma). Acute traumatic aortic rupture must be prioritized—it commonly presents with sudden dyspnea, confusion (from hypotension/shock), and minimal external signs; mortality exceeds 80% without rapid intervention. Flail chest with pulmonary contusion fits the mechanism and respiratory distress, though it typically causes more localized pain and paradoxical breathing—still highly plausible. Intra-abdominal hemorrhage (e.g., splenic or hepatic laceration) is likely but slightly less immediately life-threatening than the top three; hypovolemic shock would explain both mental status changes and respiratory distress (tachypnea from metabolic acidosis and compensatory effort), though abdominal signs are not yet reported."}
